Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Sapphire Sleet trojanized npm payload hashes on disk / in-execution · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Sapphire Sleet npm supply-chain C2 egress to npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Sapphire Sleet npm supply-chain C2 egress to npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections and DNS lookups to the Sapphire Sleet (BlueNoroff) command-and-control infrastructure used by the trojanized debug/chalk/axios npm packages: the typosquat domain npmjs.store and the IP 216.74.123.126. Article-specific because it keys on the exact C2 IOCs Amazon attributed to this DPRK campaign, not a generic beacon shape. Rationale: Uses the two hard C2 IOCs Amazon published for this campaign (npmjs.store typosquat + 216.74.123.126); both are attacker-controlled infra with no legitimate use, so a single hit is high fidelity. Corroborated by The Hacker News and The Register. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/amazon-links-debug-and-chalk-npm-hijack.html • https://www.scworld.com/news/amazon-attributes-axios-debug-chalk-npm-attacks-to-dprks-sapphire-sleet • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/30/amazon-links-four-poisoned-npm-packages-to-one-north-korean-crew/5281120 • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0108/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or threat-intel analyst deliberately detonating the malicious package in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • DNS sinkhole / RPZ appliance logging the blocked lookup to npmjs.store (appears as a resolution attempt)
  • A proxy/secure-web-gateway pre-fetching or category-checking the domain rather than an actual client beacon
  • Typo by a developer typing npmjs.store instead of npmjs.com in a browser (rare, but produces a DNS-only hit with no post-install process context)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if it is node.exe/npm/npx or a post-install script child, treat as confirmed supply-chain execution; capture the resolved IP, port and the package being installed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block npmjs.store and 216.74.123.126 at egress, and freeze any credentials/tokens (npm, cloud, wallet) that were reachable from that developer/CI context. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host that installed debug/chalk/axios/typo-crypto in the affected version window, sweep for the payload hashes (companion UC), and audit CI/CD runners and lockfiles for the malicious versions.
let c2ip = "216.74.123.126";
let c2dom = "npmjs.store";
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == c2ip or RemoteUrl has c2dom
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where RemoteUrl has c2dom or AdditionalFields has c2dom
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl)
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2ip = "216.74.123.126";
let c2dom = "npmjs.store";
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == c2ip or DestinationHostName has c2dom or RequestURL has c2dom
| project TimeGenerated, Source=SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, ProcessName, DeviceProduct),
(DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has c2dom
| project TimeGenerated, Source=ClientIP, DestinationIP=RemoteIp, DestinationHostName=Name, Computer)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Sapphire Sleet npm C2 DNS/Connection (npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126)
id: 8f2a1c94-7d3e-4b1a-9c0f-2e6d5a4b7c11
description: Detects DNS resolution or network connection to the Sapphire Sleet npm supply-chain C2 (typosquat domain npmjs.store or IP 216.74.123.126).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/amazon-links-debug-chalk-npm-supply-chain-attacks-to-north-korean-hackers/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/amazon-links-debug-and-chalk-npm-hijack.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection_domain:
    QueryName|contains: 'npmjs.store'
  selection_ip:
    Answers|contains: '216.74.123.126'
  condition: selection_domain or selection_ip
level: high
source:windows.sysmon ((@EventID:3 AND (@DestinationIp:216.74.123.126 OR @DestinationHostname:(*npmjs.store* OR *NPMJS.STORE*))) OR (@EventID:22 AND @QueryName:(*npmjs.store* OR *NPMJS.STORE*)))
#event_simpleName=/^(DnsRequest|NetworkConnectIP4)$/ (DomainName=/npmjs\.store/i OR RemoteAddressIP4="216.74.123.126")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="216.74.123.126" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="npmjs.store" OR All_Traffic.url="*npmjs.store*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.url | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="216.74.123.126" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="npmjs.store" OR All_Traffic.url="*npmjs.store*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.url | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Sapphire Sleet trojanized npm payload hashes on disk / in-execution AIInstallation High
Detects the two known-bad SHA256 payloads tied to the Sapphire Sleet npm supply-chain compromise landing on disk or executing, across file-write and process-creation telemetry. Article-specific because it pins to the exact malware hashes Amazon attributed to the debug/chalk/axios trojanization, indicating a compromised package was installed and its post-install stage ran. Rationale: Pins to the two SHA256 payload hashes Amazon published for the debug/chalk/axios trojanization; a file-write or process-exec match is a near-certain compromised-package indicator with negligible false positives. Attribution and TTP (post-install hooks) corroborated by SC Media and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/amazon-links-debug-and-chalk-npm-hijack.html • https://www.scworld.com/news/amazon-attributes-axios-debug-chalk-npm-attacks-to-dprks-sapphire-sleet • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0108/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis / detonation lab intentionally handling the sample
  • EDR or AV quarantine copy of the file being written to a vault path (still worth reviewing but not an active infection)
  • Threat-intel hash-set validation testing on a sanctioned host
  • Backup/imaging software copying an already-quarantined artifact between hosts
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\MpArchive"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash hit is a live drop/exec (not an AV quarantine path) and identify the parent — node.exe/npm post-install indicates the trojanized package ran; record the package name and version. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and revoke npm tokens, cloud credentials and crypto-wallet material accessible from that context (Sapphire Sleet is financially motivated). 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints and CI runners for the same hashes and for the companion C2 egress to npmjs.store/216.74.123.126, and pin lockfiles to known-good versions of debug, chalk, axios and typo-crypto.
let badHashes = dynamic(["24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f","2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73"]);
union
(DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where SHA256 in (badHashes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="FileEvent", ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where SHA256 in (badHashes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="ProcessEvent", ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
let badHashes = dynamic(["24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f","2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in (badHashes)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, Hash=TargetFileSHA256),
(ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where SHA256 in (badHashes)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName=ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath=TargetProcessName, Hash=SHA256)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or SHA1 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or MD5 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or SHA1 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or MD5 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VMware fixes three critical flaws allowing auth bypass, VM escapes

BleepingComputer
2026-07-30 6 use cases 1 technique 4 kill-chain phases detected

Broadcom has released security updates to fix five vulnerabilities in VMware vCenter, ESX, Workstation, and Fusion, including three critical flaws that allow attackers to bypass authentication, execute arbitrary code, or escape from a virtual machine to the host. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] VMware ESX/vCenter hosts exposed to VMSA-2026-0006 critical CVEs (59309/59310/47876)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ESXi rogue/'ghost' VM instantiated from the shell (VirtualGHOST persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
VMware ESX/vCenter hosts exposed to VMSA-2026-0006 critical CVEs (59309/59310/47876) AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed assets whose installed VMware vCenter/ESX/Workstation/Fusion build is still vulnerable to the five VMSA-2026-0006 CVEs, using the exact CVE identifiers from the advisory. Article-specific because it pins the concrete CVE IDs and VMware products Broadcom flagged as emergency changes with no workaround. Rationale: Uses the five concrete CVE IDs from Broadcom VMSA-2026-0006 (CVE-2026-59309/59310/47876/41703/41709) against vulnerability-management telemetry — zero-FP asset exposure query since the match is on the exact CVE and VMware vendor string; internet-facing join prioritises the unauthenticated 9.8 vCenter flaws. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-critical-vmware-vcenter-vulnerabilities-allow-authentication-bypass-and-remote-code-execution-cve-2026-59309-cve-2026-59310/ • https://support.broadcom.com/web/ecx/support-content-notification/-/external/content/SecurityAdvisories/0/38017 • https://threatprotect.qualys.com/2026/07/30/vmware-esx-vcenter-workstation-and-fusion-multiple-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched to fixed build (vCenter 9.1.0.0300 / 9.0.2.0100 / 8.0 U3k, ESXi 9.1.0.0200 / 9.0.2.0100 / 8.0 U3k) but scanner cache is stale
  • Decommissioned vCenter/ESXi appliance still in the asset inventory
  • Workstation/Fusion 25H2 flagged for CVE-2026-41703 where impact is only Low info-disclosure, not the critical set
  • Third-party product bundling vCenter/ESX (Cloud Foundation, Telco Cloud) reported under a different SoftwareName
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !in ("9.1.0.0300","9.0.2.0100","8.0 U3k","9.1.0.0200")
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort results by IsInternetFacing/severity and confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely below the VMSA-2026-0006 fixed build; prioritise any network-reachable vCenter (CVE-2026-59309/59310, unauth 9.8). 2) Contain: restrict management-plane (443/vSphere Client, syslog) access to admin jump hosts via firewall/NSX while scheduling the emergency patch; use vMotion + rolling reboot for ESXi, power down non-migratable VMs. 3) Hunt: on any vulnerable vCenter, pivot to UC2 (rogue/ghost VM persistence) and review VMware Directory Service / vpxd auth logs for anomalous unauthenticated access preceding the patch window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-59309","CVE-2026-59310","CVE-2026-47876","CVE-2026-41703","CVE-2026-41709")
| where SoftwareVendor has_any ("vmware","broadcom")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| sort by IsInternetFacing desc, CveId asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-59309","CVE-2026-59310","CVE-2026-47876","CVE-2026-41703","CVE-2026-41709")
| where SoftwareVendor has_any ("vmware","broadcom")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by CveId asc

ESXi rogue/'ghost' VM instantiated from the shell (VirtualGHOST persistence) AIInstallation Low
Hunts ESXi host syslog (shell.log/hostd) for virtual machines being registered or powered on directly from the command line rather than through vCenter/vpxa — the VirtualGHOST persistence technique the article cites as the reason compromised vCenter/ESX matters. Targets vim-cmd VM lifecycle operations that create unregistered VMs invisible to the vCenter/ESXi console. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit VirtualGHOST reference; hunts the exact ESXi shell operations (vim-cmd solo/registervm, vim-cmd vmsvc/power.on) CrowdStrike documents for powering on VMs outside the vCenter inventory to evade logging (MITRE T1564.006 / T1673). Deliberately hunting-tier — legitimate ESXi CLI admin use is common, so it needs analyst correlation with an unregistered-VM check. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/CrowdStrike/VirtualGHOST • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1673/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/falcon-next-gen-siem-protects-against-vmware-vcenter-attacks/
ATT&CKT1564.006 T1673
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin registering/powering a VM from ESXi shell during vCenter outage or DR
  • Backup/replication tooling (Veeam, SRM) invoking vim-cmd vmsvc operations
  • Automation scripts running esxcli vm process list for inventory/health checks
  • Break-glass ESXi host maintenance where vpxa/vCenter management is temporarily bypassed
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each host, run 'vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms' vs 'esxcli vm process list | grep Display' — a powered-on VM present in esxcli but absent from vim-cmd inventory confirms a ghost VM; correlate the shell command's timestamp/source IP with authorised admin change windows. 2) Contain: if unregistered, isolate the ESXi host's management interface, snapshot the rogue .vmx/.vmdk for forensics, and suspend the ghost VM (do not delete before imaging). 3) Hunt: review DCUI/SSH enablement and shell.log for the session that spawned it, check vpxd auth logs for the preceding vCenter access, and run CrowdStrike Detect-VirtualGHOST across the whole cluster to find sibling ghosts.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName in~ ("shell","hostd","vmsvc","Vpxa") or Facility in~ ("shell","daemon","user")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("vim-cmd solo/registervm","vim-cmd vmsvc/power.on","vim-cmd vmsvc/reload","esxcli vm process list")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

("vim-cmd solo/registervm" OR "vim-cmd vmsvc/power.on" OR "vim-cmd vmsvc/reload" OR "esxcli vm process list")
| rex field=_raw "(?<esxi_cmd>vim-cmd\s+\S+|esxcli\s+vm\s+process\s+\S+)"
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(esxi_cmd) as commands values(source) as logfile by host

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-59309", "CVE-2026-59310", "CVE-2026-47876", "CVE-2026-41703", "CVE-2026-41709")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Successful Entra ID device-code authentication (ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS MFA bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts successful OAuth device-code grant sign-ins in Entra ID, the flow abused by the ARToken/EvilTokens phishing-as-a-service platform to bypass MFA and mint persistent refresh tokens. Device-code auth is rare/unused in most tenants, so any success warrants review for account takeover. Rationale: Grounds on the ARToken/EvilTokens device-code phishing pattern named in the corroborated Talos IR Q2 2026 report; device-code auth success is inherently rare and high-signal for token-theft AiTM. Cross-checked https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-in from IoT/kiosk/CLI tooling (Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code')
  • Conference-room / smart-TV Teams device provisioning
  • Developers using device-code flow for headless service auth
  • PowerShell modules (Microsoft.Graph, Az) prompting device-code login on servers
Suppression filter
| where ClientAppUsed !in ("Mobile Apps and Desktop clients") or Application !has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools")
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each hit, confirm whether the user legitimately performs device-code logins; check the IP/geo/ASN and UserAgent against the user's baseline and look for impossible travel. 2) Contain: If unrecognized, revoke sessions/refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and re-register MFA; block the source IP. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the AccountUpn for subsequent non-interactive token use, new inbox rules, OAuth app consents, and mailbox/SharePoint access from the same IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0            // successful device-code grant
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ResultType == 0           // successful device-code grant
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized MeshAgent running outside its install path (Sinobi ransomware C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts MeshAgent / MeshCentral processes executing from non-standard locations, the trojanized SYSTEM-level auto-start C2 used by Sinobi ransomware operators. Legitimate MeshCentral installs live under a fixed program path; execution elsewhere indicates an attacker-deployed agent. Rationale: Uses the corroborated report detail that Sinobi deployed a trojanized MeshAgent as SYSTEM auto-start C2; anchoring on the MeshAgent binary/product plus a path-exclusion turns a legit tool into a high-fidelity attacker signal. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026 and detection.fyi renamed-MeshAgent Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/macos/process_creation/proc_creation_macos_remote_access_tools_renamed_meshagent_execution/
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned MeshCentral deployment installed to a custom directory by IT
  • Portable MeshAgent run from a technician's USB during legitimate support
  • Security-team red-team or RMM evaluation testing
  • MSP-managed endpoints where MeshCentral is the approved RMM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("approved-rmm-svc") and SHA256 !in ("<known-good-meshagent-sha256-from-your-approved-build>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Verify whether MeshCentral is an approved RMM for this host/business unit; inspect the file path, SHA256 (reputation), signer, and the parent process that dropped it. 2) Contain: If unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the MeshAgent service/process, and block its outbound WSS destination at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: Search other hosts for the same SHA256/service, look for co-located ransomware staging (rclone.exe, GPO logon scripts, .SINOBI files) and enumerate the account that installed the service.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "meshagent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName has "MeshAgent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "MeshCentral"
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Mesh Agent\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "meshagent"
| where NewProcessName !has @"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment (Warlock / Storm-2603 ransomware) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of Zoho Assist Unattended Agent binaries, the RMM tool Warlock (Storm-2603) operators install for persistent, session-independent remote control ahead of encryption. Flags the agent/installer binaries especially when run non-interactively or as SYSTEM. Rationale: Anchors on the corroborated report detail that Warlock/Storm-2603 deployed the Zoho Assist Unattended Agent for persistence; the unattended/SYSTEM context distinguishes attacker deployment from interactive helpdesk use. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026 and Intel471 RMM-abuse writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/understanding-and-threat-hunting-for-rmm-software-misuse
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Zoho Assist use by an internal or outsourced IT helpdesk
  • MSP performing legitimate unattended-access provisioning
  • Software inventory/patching workflows that bundle Zoho
  • User-initiated Zoho support session for a real ticket
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("helpdesk-svc","msp-support") and DeviceName !in~ ("<known-helpdesk-hosts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether Zoho Assist is an approved support tool for this host; check who initiated it, the parent process, and whether an unattended (session-independent) install was performed. 2) Contain: If unauthorized, isolate the host, remove the Zoho Assist Unattended service, and block Zoho Assist gateway domains for the affected segment. 3) Hunt: Enumerate other hosts with the same binary/service, review for follow-on ransomware TTPs (rclone staging, shadow-copy deletion, GPO logon scripts) and audit the service account used for install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ZOHO"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Zoho Assist"
    or FileName in~ ("ZA_Access.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZMAgent.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "Zoho_Assist"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("unattended","install","silent") or ProcessIntegrityLevel == "System"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ZA_Access.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZMAgent.exe","Zoho_Assist")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email-hiding inbox rules created post-compromise (BEC / mailbox concealment) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts creation/modification of Exchange Online inbox rules that delete, mark-as-read, redirect, or move messages to hidden folders — the concealment step Talos IR observed after auth-abuse account takeover, often preceding large outbound email bursts. Distinct from generic phishing-click detections. Rationale: Grounds on the corroborated Talos IR finding of email-hiding rule creation (T1564.008) and outbound-email spikes after auth abuse; scoping to delete/redirect/mark-read parameters keeps only concealment-intent rules rather than benign filing rules. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately auto-filing newsletters into folders or Deleted Items
  • Executive assistant configuring forwarding to a shared mailbox
  • Mailbox migration/cleanup tooling that rewrites rules in bulk
  • Out-of-office or VIP triage rules marking mail as read
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "MoveToFolder" and Parameters !has_any ("DeleteMessage","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","Deleted Items"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the rule parameters and the creating IP/UserAgent against the user's baseline; check if the same session had a risky/device-code sign-in or impossible travel. 2) Contain: If malicious, remove the inbox rule, revoke sessions, reset credentials + re-register MFA, and search sent items for fraudulent/BEC messages. 3) Hunt: Correlate with outbound email volume spikes (e.g., thousands of messages), other users with identical rule patterns, and OAuth app consents from the same source IP.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Exchange Online"
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules","Update-InboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("DeleteMessage","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","Junk Email","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","Junk Email","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, OfficeWorkload, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-16232")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-16232")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Entra MFA method registered from an IP the user has never signed in from (attacker device enrollment) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Entra MFA/security-info registration fan-out from single source IP (ShinyHunters help-desk vishing)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Entra user OAuth consent to connected app (ShinyHunters Data Loader-style Salesforce grant)
Entra MFA/security-info registration fan-out from single source IP (ShinyHunters help-desk vishing) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ShinyHunters/UNC6040 vishing tell where an attacker calls the help desk or multiple employees and enrolls attacker-controlled MFA methods, producing 3+ distinct users registering security info from one source IP inside a short window. Article-specific: Brinks Home was breached via a Microsoft Entra vishing/registration flow, and mass MFA enrollment from a single origin is the highest-fidelity variant of that behaviour. Rationale: Anchored on Entra security-info-registration audit operations plus the single-source-IP fan-out threshold (>=3 users/10m) that ReliaQuest/GTIG flag as the ShinyHunters help-desk vishing signature; the article states the breach used a Microsoft Entra vishing/registration flow. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6040-proactive-hardening-recommendations • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-shinyhunters-data-breach-targets-salesforce-amid-scattered-spider-collaboration/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html
ATT&CKT1556.006 T1098.005 T1566.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT onboarding day where a technician bulk-enrolls MFA for several new hires from one help-desk workstation IP
  • Corporate NAT/proxy egress where many legitimate users register security info from a shared public IP
  • Password/MFA reset campaign after a policy change forcing re-registration
  • MDM/Intune provisioning kiosk performing device+MFA setup for multiple users
  • VPN concentrator IP aggregating remote employees during a scheduled MFA rollout
Suppression filter
| where not (IPAddress in ("10.","172.16.","192.168.") or ipv4_is_private(IPAddress)) // exclude internal help-desk/NAT; maintain an allowlist of onboarding kiosk IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's geo/ASN and confirm whether it belongs to a known corporate NAT/help-desk range; list the enrolled users and the specific auth methods added (phone/app). 2) Contain: if the IP is external/unrecognised, revoke the newly registered MFA methods, revoke refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), and force password reset for every affected user. 3) Hunt: check each user for a successful sign-in or OAuth app consent from that same IP within 1h, and query Salesforce/other SaaS SSO for access originating from these accounts post-enrollment.
let window = 10m;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft Entra ID","Office 365","Azure Active Directory")
| where ActionType in ("User registered security info.","User started security info registration.","Admin registered security info.","User registered all required security info.")
| where isnotempty(IPAddress)
| summarize DistinctUsers = dcount(AccountObjectId), Users = make_set(AccountDisplayName, 20), Ops = make_set(ActionType), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, CountryCode, bin(Timestamp, window)
| where DistinctUsers >= 3   // 3+ distinct users enrolling MFA from one IP in 10m = help-desk vishing (ReliaQuest guidance)
| order by DistinctUsers desc
let window = 10m;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Category == "UserManagement"
| where OperationName in ("User registered security info","User started security info registration","User registered all required security info","Admin registered security info","User changed default security info")
| where Result == "success"
| extend SrcIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress), TargetUser = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| where isnotempty(SrcIp)
| summarize DistinctUsers = dcount(TargetUser), Users = make_set(TargetUser, 20), Ops = make_set(OperationName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIp, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where DistinctUsers >= 3   // 3+ users enrolling MFA from one IP in 10m = help-desk vishing tell
| order by DistinctUsers desc

Entra MFA method registered from an IP the user has never signed in from (attacker device enrollment) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts single-user account takeover: an Entra security-info/MFA registration originating from an IP that does not appear in that user's prior 30 days of successful sign-ins — the moment a ShinyHunters vishing target enrolls the attacker's device. Article-specific to the Brinks Home Microsoft Entra vishing 'complete an authentication or registration process' description. Rationale: Uses Entra security-info-registration audit ops joined leftanti against the user's own 30-day known sign-in IPs, so it fires only when an MFA method is added from a never-before-seen origin — the ShinyHunters attacker-device-enrollment moment described as the Entra 'registration process' in the article. Datadog left empty: the per-user historical-IP baseline (leftanti join) cannot be expressed in a bare Datadog query. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-shinyhunters-data-breach-targets-salesforce-amid-scattered-spider-collaboration/ • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1098.005 T1566.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate employee travelling and enrolling a new authenticator from a hotel/airport IP
  • New hire's first-ever MFA registration where no prior sign-in baseline exists for the account
  • User switching ISPs or moving to a home IP not seen in the last 30 days
  • Roaming mobile registration over a cellular carrier CGNAT range
  • Admin-on-behalf registration performed for a user from an admin's workstation IP
Suppression filter
| where not (OperationName == "User registered security info" and isempty(prior_signin_count)) // suppress genuine first-ever enrollments; enrich with an IdentityInfo join on account creation date to exclude accounts < 14 days old
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the registration IP's geo/ASN and compare to the user's normal locations; ask the user (out-of-band) whether they added an authenticator and whether they took a recent 'IT support' call. 2) Contain: if unverified, delete the new MFA method, revoke sessions/refresh tokens, disable the account, and require an in-person identity check before re-enabling. 3) Hunt: pivot on the registration IP across all users (feeds UC1 fan-out), and search SigninLogs + OAuth consent (UC3) for downstream Salesforce/SaaS access from the account.
let lookback = 30d;
let recent = 2d;
let knownIps = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | summarize by AccountObjectId, IPAddress;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(recent)
| where ActionType in ("User registered security info.","Admin registered security info.","User changed default security info.","User registered all required security info.","User started security info registration.")
| where isnotempty(IPAddress) and isnotempty(AccountObjectId)
| join kind=leftanti knownIps on AccountObjectId, IPAddress
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, City, ActionType, Application
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
let recent = 2d;
let knownIps = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
    | where ResultType == 0
    | summarize by UserUpn = tolower(UserPrincipalName), IPAddress;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where OperationName in ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User changed default security info","User registered all required security info","User started security info registration")
| where Result == "success"
| extend RegIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress), UserUpn = tolower(tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName))
| where isnotempty(RegIp) and isnotempty(UserUpn)
| join kind=leftanti knownIps on UserUpn, $left.RegIp == $right.IPAddress
| project TimeGenerated, UserUpn, RegIp, OperationName, Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.action=modified (All_Changes.command="User registered security info" OR All_Changes.command="Admin registered security info" OR All_Changes.command="User changed default security info" OR All_Changes.command="User registered all required security info") by All_Changes.object All_Changes.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)`
| rename object as user, src as reg_src
| join type=left user [| tstats `summariesonly` values(Authentication.src) as known_src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success earliest=-30d@d latest=-2d@d by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`]
| eval known_match=if(isnull(known_src),0,mvcount(mvfilter(known_src=reg_src)))
| where known_match=0
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| table firstTime user reg_src
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.action=modified (All_Changes.command="User registered security info" OR All_Changes.command="Admin registered security info" OR All_Changes.command="User changed default security info" OR All_Changes.command="User registered all required security info") by All_Changes.object All_Changes.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)`
| rename object as user, src as reg_src
| join type=left user [| tstats summariesonly=false values(Authentication.src) as known_src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success earliest=-30d@d latest=-2d@d by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`]
| eval known_match=if(isnull(known_src),0,mvcount(mvfilter(known_src=reg_src)))
| where known_match=0
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| table firstTime user reg_src
Entra user OAuth consent to connected app (ShinyHunters Data Loader-style Salesforce grant) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts an end-user (not admin) granting OAuth consent to a connected/enterprise app — the UNC6040 technique of talking a vished employee through authorizing an attacker-controlled 'Data Loader' connected app to bulk-export Salesforce Contacts. Article-specific: ShinyHunters exfiltrated 1.1M+ 'Contacts' Salesforce records after the Entra vishing, and connected-app consent grants persistent API access. Rationale: Anchored on the Entra application-consent audit operations that GTIG/Mandiant document as UNC6040's malicious Data Loader connected-app grant; filtering to user-initiated (non-admin) consent isolates the vished employee action that led to the 1.1M Salesforce 'Contacts' export claimed in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6040-proactive-hardening-recommendations • https://thehackernews.com/2025/06/google-exposes-vishing-group-unc6040.html • https://www.varonis.com/blog/salesforce-vishing-threat-unc604
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee legitimately authorizing a sanctioned SaaS integration (e.g. approved Salesforce/marketing connector)
  • Developer consenting to an internal line-of-business app during testing
  • Users granting consent to well-known Microsoft first-party apps
  • Browser extension or productivity add-in consent flows
  • Tenant with user-consent enabled where low-risk read-only scopes are routinely approved
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Graph","Microsoft Office","Office 365 Exchange Online") and PropNew has_any ("offline_access","full","api","read_all","Contacts") // keep broad/persistent scopes, drop known first-party + benign read-only consents
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the consented app's publisher, app ID, and requested delegated scopes; unknown publisher + broad/offline_access or CRM/data scopes on a brand-new app = high suspicion. 2) Contain: disable/delete the enterprise app registration, revoke its OAuth2PermissionGrants and the user's refresh tokens, and (in Salesforce) revoke the connected app and rotate any exposed API/refresh tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate the consenting user against UC1/UC2 MFA-registration hits and the consent IP; review Salesforce login/API/BulkAPI export history for that user around the consent time for mass Contacts extraction.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add delegated permission grant.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ActionType, ObjectName, ActivityObjects, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Consent to application","Add delegated permission grant","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant")
| where Result == "success"
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), SrcIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress), AppDisplayName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName), Props = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties
| where isnotempty(Actor)   // user-initiated consent (vishing target), not admin/background service
| mv-expand Props
| extend PropName = tostring(Props.displayName), PropNew = tostring(Props.newValue)
| where PropName in ("ConsentAction.Permissions","DelegatedPermissionGrant.Scope","ConsentContext.IsAdminConsent") or isempty(PropName)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, SrcIp, AppDisplayName, OperationName, PropName, PropNew
| order by TimeGenerated desc
