Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

STAC4749 Teams vishing: Quick Assist / RemSupp remote-support tool spawning a shell AIDelivery High
Hunts a live remote-support session (Microsoft Quick Assist or the RemSupp RMM the STAC4749 actors steered victims to) that immediately spawns a command interpreter or download utility. This is the pivot from social-engineered remote access to hands-on-keyboard execution, unique to this campaign's Teams-vishing entry. Rationale: Uses the two named remote-access tools the actors used (Quick Assist and RemSupp) as the parent, paired with a shell/download child — the specific hands-on-keyboard pivot Sophos describes. Cross-checked Sophos X-Ops blog and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/chaos-in-teams-vishing • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-teams-vishing-attacks-lead-to-chaos-ransomware-attacks/
ATT&CKT1219 T1566.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate helpdesk running Quick Assist and launching cmd/powershell to troubleshoot
  • IT admin using RemSupp for sanctioned remote support then opening a shell
  • Managed-service-provider remote sessions that routinely open a terminal
  • Automated Quick Assist diagnostics that call curl.exe for connectivity checks
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppData","Temp","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","-enc","-w hidden") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppData","Temp","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","-enc","-w hidden")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether a Quick Assist/RemSupp session was expected — check the helpdesk ticketing system and ask the user if they received an unsolicited Teams call from 'IT support'. Review the child ProcessCommandLine for download/AppData strings. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the remote-support process tree, and block the associated external Teams tenant/domain at the perimeter. Reset the user's credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on DeviceName for follow-on PowerShell downloads to %AppData%, Realtek/WinAudio Run-key writes, and DWAgent/AnyDesk installs across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("quickassist.exe","remsupp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("QuickAssist.exe","quickassist.exe","RemSupp.exe","remsupp.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe")
| where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

STAC4749 PowerShell backdoor download into %AppData% (updater.exe / helper / msupdate.exe) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the STAC4749 execution step where, after remote access, PowerShell downloads a loader/backdoor (named updater.exe, helper*.exe, msupdate.exe per Sophos) into %AppData% or %Temp% and unblocks it. Targets the download primitive plus the campaign-specific drop names and Unblock-File usage. Rationale: Article states PowerShell was used to download a backdoor into %AppData%; the Sophos Tactical Evolution diagram names updater.exe/helper*/msupdate.exe loader-backdoor filenames — combined with the download cmdlet + Unblock-File this is high-fidelity for the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/chaos-in-teams-vishing • https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/security/s/STAC4749/STAC4749Chaos2607.png
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software updaters invoking PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest into AppData
  • Developer/admin scripts using Start-BitsTransfer to stage tooling
  • Chocolatey/winget install scripts downloading to Temp
  • Security tooling that calls Unblock-File after downloading signed content
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("quickassist.exe","remsupp.exe","cmd.exe","explorer.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".top","Unblock-File")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the full command line, extract the download URL and destination path; check if the URL is a known-good vendor or an IT-themed .top domain. Retrieve and hash the dropped binary. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the dropped file, isolate the host, and block the download URL/domain. Submit the sample for analysis. Step 3 (hunt): Search DeviceRegistryEvents for a Realtek/WinAudio Run-key pointing at the dropped path and DeviceNetworkEvents for Golang-implant C2 beacons from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","Invoke-RestMethod","DownloadFile","DownloadString","Start-BitsTransfer")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppData","Unblock-File","updater.exe","msupdate.exe","helper")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","Invoke-RestMethod","DownloadFile","DownloadString","Start-BitsTransfer")
| where CommandLine has_any ("AppData","Unblock-File","updater.exe","msupdate.exe","helper")
| where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

STAC4749 Run-key persistence disguised as Realtek / WinAudio audio components AIInstallation High
Hunts registry Run/RunOnce persistence whose value name masquerades as a Realtek or Windows audio component ('Realtek HD Audio', 'Realtek Audio UHD', 'Realtek HD Audio Universal Service', 'Realtek Audio', 'WinAudio life2') pointing at a backdoor in AppData/Temp. This masquerade is a defining STAC4749 persistence artefact. Rationale: The article and Sophos diagram name the exact masquerade value strings ('Realtek HD Audio', 'Realtek Audio UHD', 'WinAudio life2', etc.) written to Run keys — audio components have no business in a Run key, making value-name masquerade high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/chaos-in-teams-vishing • https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/security/s/STAC4749/STAC4749Chaos2607.png
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Realtek audio driver installer writing a differently-named autostart (rare in Run key)
  • OEM bloatware audio utilities on new laptop images
  • Legit vendor updaters that occasionally register audio helper autoruns
Suppression filter
| where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\") or (RegistryValueData !has @"\Program Files" and RegistryValueData !has @"\Windows\System32")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect RegistryValueData — a legit Realtek entry points into Program Files/System32; a STAC4749 entry points into %AppData% or %Temp%. Hash the referenced binary. Step 2 (contain): Delete the Run value, quarantine the referenced binary, isolate the host, and reset the affected user's credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the estate for the same value names and for the DWAgent/AnyDesk installs and .top C2 that accompany Chaos deployment.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("Realtek HD Audio","Realtek Audio UHD","Realtek HD Audio Universal Service","Realtek Audio","WinAudio life2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
| where RegistryValue in~ ("Realtek HD Audio","Realtek Audio UHD","Realtek HD Audio Universal Service","Realtek Audio","WinAudio life2")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

STAC4749 backup-access RMM (DWAgent/AnyDesk) install + RDP enablement for lateral movement AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the STAC4749 lateral-movement prep: installing DWAgent or AnyDesk as backup remote access and enabling RDP (setting fDenyTSConnections=0 via reg.exe or opening the Remote Desktop firewall rule via netsh). Fires when these appear on a host already touched by the vishing chain. Rationale: Article names DWAgent and AnyDesk as backup access and states the actors enabled RDP to move laterally; fDenyTSConnections=0 and the netsh Remote Desktop firewall rule are the concrete registry/command artefacts of RDP enablement. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/chaos-in-teams-vishing • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-teams-vishing-attacks-lead-to-chaos-ransomware-attacks/
ATT&CKT1219 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT department legitimately deploying AnyDesk/DWAgent as a sanctioned support tool
  • Sysadmin enabling RDP on a jump host via reg/netsh during provisioning
  • Group Policy or an MDM baseline toggling Remote Desktop firewall rules
  • Helpdesk enabling RDP for a work-from-home user with a ticket
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("quickassist.exe","remsupp.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Correlate the host/timestamp with an inbound Quick Assist/RemSupp session and any Realtek/WinAudio Run-key write in the prior hours; check if the RMM install or RDP change was ticketed. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate the host, uninstall the RMM agent, revert fDenyTSConnections to 1, and disable the Remote Desktop firewall rule; reset credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate inbound RDP (LogonType 10) from this host to others and look for readme.chaos.txt drops and simultaneous encryption activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("dwagent.exe","anydesk.exe"))
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections")
    or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("firewall","Remote Desktop"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName has_any ("dwagent.exe","anydesk.exe"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "reg.exe" and CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "netsh.exe" and CommandLine has_all ("firewall","Remote Desktop"))
| where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

STAC4749 IT-themed .top C2 / lure domain contact (sequrityupdate.top et al.) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/network contact to the STAC4749 IT-support-themed .top domains used for Teams-vishing lures and infrastructure: sequrityupdate.top, scan-security.top, system-connect.top, corp-connect.top, supportsoft.top. Any resolution of these from a managed host is high-signal for this campaign. Rationale: The five .top domains are named IOCs in the article and corroborated by the Sophos blog and the DFIR Radar summary; a .top IT-themed domain resolving from an endpoint is high-fidelity for STAC4749 infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/chaos-in-teams-vishing • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-teams-vishing-attacks-lead-to-chaos-ransomware-attacks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/analyst sandbox intentionally resolving the IOC domains
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling pre-resolving IOCs
  • A benign unrelated site squatting on an expired one of these domains after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host and the InitiatingProcess that made the request — a browser click vs a backdoor beacon changes severity. Confirm the domain is still attacker-controlled (not sinkholed). Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block all five domains at DNS and proxy, isolate any host that beaconed (non-browser process), and reset the user's credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the resolved IP to find other beaconing hosts, and check those hosts for Realtek Run-key persistence and Chaos ransom notes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("sequrityupdate.top","scan-security.top","system-connect.top","corp-connect.top","supportsoft.top")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("sequrityupdate.top","scan-security.top","system-connect.top","corp-connect.top","supportsoft.top")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

STAC4749 Chaos ransomware note (readme.chaos.txt) creation across hosts AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the impact stage: creation of the Chaos ransomware note 'readme.chaos.txt' on endpoints. Because STAC4749 encrypts simultaneously across compromised devices, mass creation of this exact note name is a definitive, alerting-grade signal of active Chaos deployment. Rationale: The article states Chaos ransom notes are named 'readme.chaos.txt' and are dropped on affected systems during simultaneous encryption — an exact, campaign-specific filename that is unambiguous impact evidence. Cross-checked BleepingComputer and Sophos. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-teams-vishing-attacks-lead-to-chaos-ransomware-attacks/ • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/chaos-in-teams-vishing
ATT&CKT1486 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware sample detonation in a sanctioned analysis VM producing the note
  • Purple-team/BAS exercise dropping a benign copy of the ransom note
  • Backup of a previously-encrypted file set being restored to a share (note copied along)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Treat as a live-encryption incident — confirm on the host whether files are being renamed/encrypted alongside the note and identify InitiatingProcess. Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate all hosts showing the note, kill the encrypting process, disable the compromised accounts, and invoke the ransomware IR plan / preserve for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate every host with readme.chaos.txt, check for prior data staging/exfil (the actors likely stole data first), vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion, and the upstream Teams-vishing entry point.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "readme.chaos.txt"
| summarize NoteCount = count(), Folders = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "readme.chaos.txt"
| summarize NoteCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Chaos Ransomware Note readme.chaos.txt Created (STAC4749)

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |

    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - 'Invoke-Expression'

            - 'DownloadString'

            - '-NoProfile'

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flyto2 flyto-verification unauthenticated POST /run on :8344 (CVE-2026-67426 SSRF entry) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST to the /run endpoint of the flyto-verification service on TCP 8344 from non-loopback/remote sources. The shipped Dockerfile binds 0.0.0.0:8344 and /run has no auth dependency, so any remote POST /run is the unauthenticated entry point for the callback_url SSRF and runner-secret exfiltration chain. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete endpoint (POST /run) and the Dockerfile-shipped port 8344 (verification_service.py:363-364, Dockerfile.verification CMD). Restricting to external/remote sources leverages the fix guidance ('bind loopback by default') to separate attack traffic from legit internal callers. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory confirming the 0.0.0.0:8344 exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-67426
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal verification jobs POSTing /run from an app tier reachable via a public NAT egress IP
  • Vulnerability scanners / ASM tools probing the /run path on 8344
  • Load-balancer or uptime health checks hitting /run
  • Developer testing the verification service from a bastion/VPN with a public source IP
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("<known-healthcheck-ip>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not an expected internal caller; pull the full request (body should contain callback_url/workflowYaml) from app or proxy logs and check whether the host is running flyto-core <= 2.26.6. 2) Contain: rebind flyto-verification to loopback (or firewall 8344 to internal only), and rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET immediately since it may already be exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 — search for outbound connections from the verification host to 169.254.169.254 or to any public IP, and audit engine-callback authentications using the (now-possibly-leaked) runner secret.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8344
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8344
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/run"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(SourceIP startswith "10." or SourceIP startswith "192.168." or SourceIP startswith "172.16." or SourceIP startswith "127.")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification SSRF to cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) — runner-secret/IMDS theft AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound connections from the flyto-verification runner (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/flyto-verification) to cloud instance-metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, 100.100.100.200, metadata.google.internal). CVE-2026-67426's callback_url bypasses the target_allowed allowlist and SSRF guard, letting an attacker force the service to POST to the IMDS with a controlled body and harvest instance credentials. Rationale: The article explicitly names 'cloud-metadata IP' as an SSRF target; MITRE T1552.005 and Elastic's prebuilt IMDS-SSRF rule confirm 169.254.169.254 (plus Alibaba 100.100.100.200 / GCP metadata.google.internal) as the canonical endpoints. Scoping to the python/flyto-verification process removes legit cloud-agent IMDS calls, making a web-runner->IMDS connection a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/credential_access_web_server_cloud_imds_ssrf_request • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate flyto workflow that intentionally targets an internal 169.254.x host as a callback (rare/misconfig)
  • Cloud SDK embedded in the same python venv making a genuine IMDSv2 token call for the app's own role
  • Security testing / red-team validation of the SSRF fix
  • Sidecar or observability agent sharing the process name 'python' reaching metadata for instance tags
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flyto", "verification")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is the flyto-verification runner and capture the destination path/body; check IMDS access logs (if IMDSv2 enabled) for a token issuance from this host at the same time. 2) Contain: rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET and any instance-role credentials that IMDS could have returned; enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) and block 169.254.0.0/16 egress from the container; upgrade flyto-core to 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail/AAD/GCP audit for use of the instance-role or managed-identity credentials from unexpected IPs shortly after this event, and check UC3 for the secret being POSTed to an external attacker host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "flyto-verification", "flyto")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or DstHostname has "metadata.google.internal"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification runner egress to external public host — FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the flyto-verification/python runner initiating outbound connections to public (non-RFC1918, non-link-local) destinations. Because callback_url is attacker-controlled and the service unconditionally attaches X-Internal-Key: $FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, any egress from this backend runner to an arbitrary internet host is a candidate secret-exfiltration callback. Rationale: Grounded in the sink from the advisory: post_callback -> session.post(callback_url, headers={'X-Internal-Key': FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET}) (verification_service.py:330-335). A backend verification runner that is only supposed to call the internal engine should never egress to a public IP, so process-scoped public egress is a high-value exfiltration hunt for the leaked runner secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jx74-cqjv-2c67 • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-67428
ATT&CKT1567 T1552
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate engine callback endpoint hosted on a public IP / SaaS domain rather than internal
  • Python dependency/package fetches (pip, telemetry SDKs) from the same runner venv
  • Outbound calls to a public webhook/notification service used by real workflows
  • CDN or object-storage uploads the workflow performs as designed
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "pypi.org" and RemoteUrl !has "pythonhosted.org"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the public RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and compare against the documented internal engine callback host; if it is unknown/attacker-looking, capture the flow and any TLS SNI. 2) Contain: block egress from the flyto-verification container except to the known engine, rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, and upgrade to flyto-core 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (inbound POST /run carrying that callback_url) and UC2 (IMDS access), and review engine-callback auth logs for forged authenticated callbacks using the leaked X-Internal-Key.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("flyto-verification", "flyto")) or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flyto")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OctLurk and SilkLurk: newly identified tailored backdoors in cyber-espionage cam
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OctLurk persistence: 'GoogleUpDate' scheduled task executing Videos\1.bat · [LLM] OctLurk/LurkProxy service DLL side-load via RegisterService ServiceMain · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to campaign infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OctLurk Command Shell plugin post-compromise recon cluster (chcp 1256 + session enum) · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OctLurk persistence: 'GoogleUpDate' scheduled task executing Videos\1.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the OctLurk deployment technique where the actor creates a scheduled task named GoogleUpDate that runs, once, as SYSTEM, a batch script staged at C:\Users\<user>\Videos\1.bat. That batch script (MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a) creates the malicious service that side-loads the loader DLL. Article-specific because the task name masquerades as a Google updater but launches a .bat from the Videos folder — a combination legitimate updaters never use. Rationale: Anchors on two exact article strings: the task name 'GoogleUpDate' and the payload path '\Videos\1.bat' (MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a). A batch file in a media folder driven by a fake Google-update task is unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Google Update tasks are named 'GoogleUpdateTaskMachine*' and run GoogleUpdate.exe from Program Files — never a .bat in Videos, so overlap is minimal
  • An admin scripting an ad-hoc scheduled task that happens to reference a file literally named 1.bat under a user profile
  • Software-deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) staging batch scripts in unusual user folders
  • Red-team/pentest persistence tests mimicking updater task names
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the scheduled task XML (Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName GoogleUpDate) and the 1.bat contents; confirm the task runs as SYSTEM, once, and creates a service. Hash 1.bat against MD5 6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a. 2) Contain: Disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and block the loader DLL and its service (see the service-creation UC). 3) Hunt: Sweep the estate for the same task name and for the follow-on services (NgcCIntSvc, Cusrxsrv, etc.) and beacons to the OctLurk C2 domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or CommandLine has "\\Videos\\1.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/LurkProxy service DLL side-load via RegisterService ServiceMain AIInstallation High
Hunts the service-based persistence where a batch script (1.bat / auto.bat) registers a Windows service whose ServiceMain registry value points to the 'RegisterService' export of a loader DLL (oleasapi.dll, msbasesysdc.dll). Detects both the anomalous ServiceMain=RegisterService registry write and the campaign's distinctive service names. Article-specific: legitimate svchost DLL services never name their entry point 'RegisterService'. Rationale: Uses the exact loader DLL names (oleasapi.dll, msbasesysdc.dll), the anomalous ServiceMain export 'RegisterService', and the clearly-malicious service names (NgcCIntSvc, Cusrxsrv, specitsrc, cmtastsvc). ServiceMain naming its entry point RegisterService is not a legitimate pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://www.cryptika.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog-steal-passwords-and-control-government-computers/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vendor product legitimately naming a service ServiceDll export 'RegisterService' (rare but possible for custom svchost DLL services)
  • Hyper-V integration services (vmic*) and PNRPHostSvc are legitimate names — excluded here to avoid FPs, only the non-standard names are matched
  • Endpoint agents that write to Services keys during install (match narrowed to the two loader DLL names)
  • Backup/imaging tools that re-create service registry keys during restore
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Open the flagged service registry key, note the ServiceDll path and hash the DLL (compare to oleasapi.dll 082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069). Identify the parent process that wrote the key (1.bat/auto.bat/cmd.exe). 2) Contain: Stop and delete the service, quarantine the loader DLL, isolate the host — the loader reflectively injects the backdoor into memory so a memory capture before reboot is valuable. 3) Hunt: Search for the sibling service names across the fleet and for beacons to the campaign C2 (next UC); pull the batch scripts to find the admin credentials used for remote task/service creation.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceMain" and RegistryValueData =~ "RegisterService")
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceDll" and RegistryValueData has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceName in~ ("NgcCIntSvc","Cusrxsrv","specitsrc","cmtastsvc")
    or ServiceFileName has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections to the hard-coded OctLurk, SilkLurk and LurkProxy C2 domains and IP addresses over TLS/443 (and the LurkProxy connectivity pre-check to dns.ssentialserv.xyz -> 154.196.162.76). Article-specific: these are the exact backdoor domains/IPs published in the Kaspersky IOC set. Rationale: Exact FQDNs and IPs from the published IOC list, matched on full hostnames (not the parent dynamic-DNS providers gleeze.com/kozow.com) to avoid collateral. Includes the LurkProxy pre-check domain dns.ssentialserv.xyz -> 154.196.162.76. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/ • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • digital.leroymerlin.com resembles the legitimate Leroy Merlin retailer domain — verify the resolved IP against the IOC list before escalating on that hostname alone
  • Shared hosting / VPS IPs (Vultr/Choopa ranges like 95.179.x, 45.77.x) may later be reassigned to benign tenants — decays over time
  • Security scanners or threat-intel enrichment tools deliberately resolving IOC domains
  • An analyst workstation browsing to the IOCs during investigation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in (c2Ips)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process for the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName) — expect svchost.exe hosting the malicious service, or a LurkProxy process. Confirm TLS/443 and beaconing cadence. 2) Contain: Block the domains/IPs at the proxy and perimeter firewall, isolate any beaconing host. 3) Hunt: For each host, pivot to the loader service and GoogleUpDate task UCs, and check for LurkProxy listening on port 64980 and follow-on tooling (fscan, secretsdump, Pandora RC agent).
let c2Domains = dynamic(["dns.multitoconference.com","tj.tajikistandip.com","fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com","confbase.mdpsupport.net","digital.leroymerlin.com","api2.annoyingremote.com","about.blsouqs.com","ssl.blsouqs.com","dns.ssentialserv.xyz","tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com","wedfcvbn.gleeze.com","rgnojb.casacam.net","ctyuhjerf.kozow.com","uyhvfredc.accesscam.org","gycudore.kozow.com"]);
let c2Ips = dynamic(["45.138.157.165","154.196.162.76","95.179.210.138","45.77.136.228","95.179.141.26","45.32.152.50","212.11.39.138","195.86.120.2","154.196.187.73","45.61.149.112","64.7.198.130"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (c2Domains) or RemoteIP in (c2Ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["dns.multitoconference.com","tj.tajikistandip.com","fm01.clouddevicemetrics.com","confbase.mdpsupport.net","digital.leroymerlin.com","api2.annoyingremote.com","about.blsouqs.com","ssl.blsouqs.com","dns.ssentialserv.xyz","tyhbgtyuj.gleeze.com","wedfcvbn.gleeze.com","rgnojb.casacam.net","ctyuhjerf.kozow.com","uyhvfredc.accesscam.org","gycudore.kozow.com"]);

union

| order by TimeGenerated desc
