Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

GenieLocker Windows PE encryptor: secret hex arg + genie_encrypt --percent/--recursive flags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of the GenieLocker Windows ransomware binary, which requires a long hex 'secret argument' as its first parameter and exposes the distinctive genie_encrypt CLI (-p/--percent, -r/--recursive, -l/--log). Anchored on the confirmed Windows MD5 and the unique long-form flag combination that no legitimate tool shares. Rationale: Uses the confirmed Windows MD5 (5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c) plus the genie_encrypt help-screen flags (--percent/--recursive/--log) and the mandatory hex 'secret argument' pattern extracted from the article and screenshot genielocker1.png. The long-form flag pairing is unique to this family. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/07/29164506/genielocker1.png
ATT&CKT1486 T1480.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/archive utilities that accept a --recursive flag but not alongside --percent
  • Custom internal file-processing scripts using -p and -r short flags coincidentally
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned sandbox
  • Data-migration tools invoked with long hex job IDs as the first positional argument
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","robocopy.exe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent process; confirm the hex first-argument + --percent/--recursive shape and check MD5 against 5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c. Note the encryption target path passed as the last argument. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host immediately, kill the process tree, and preserve the log file specified by -l/--log for the secret argument value. 3) Hunt: search for the same binary/flags deployed by PsExec/PAExec across other hosts (mass-deployment), and pivot to C2 IP 89.125.66.101 and KeePassXC/.kdbx access on the same accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where MD5 == "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--log")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b[0-9a-f]{32,}\b\s+(-p|--percent)\s+\d"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where (MD5 =~ "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c")
   or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
   or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "--log")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b[0-9a-f]{32,}\b\s+(-p|--percent)\s+\d"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, MD5
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi: genie_encrypt CLI execution AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ELF build of GenieLocker used to encrypt Linux servers and ESXi datastore disks after stopping running VMs. Anchored on the same cross-platform genie_encrypt usage string and --percent/--recursive/--log flags observed in the binary help output. Rationale: The help-screen usage string 'genie_encrypt [options] [path]' and the -p/-r/-l flags (image genielocker1.png) are shared by the ELF build, which the article states was used to stop VMs and encrypt ESXi/Linux disks. genie_encrypt as a command token is a near-unique anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/amp/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/07/29164506/genielocker1.png
ATT&CKT1486 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal tool literally named genie_encrypt (extremely unlikely)
  • Backup jobs invoking a recursive percentage-based sampler
  • Admin running a disk utility with --recursive on ESXi shell for maintenance
  • Security team replaying the ELF sample in an isolated lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the affected ESXi/Linux host, capture the full command line and the last positional path argument (encryption target) and confirm running-VM state changes preceding it. 2) Contain: isolate the host/datastore, halt the process, and protect ESXi snapshots/backups from the same actor. 3) Hunt: check for SSH lateral movement into other Linux/ESXi hosts, the reverse SSH tunnel to 89.125.66.101, and the same genie_encrypt invocation across the cluster.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "genie_encrypt"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "genie_encrypt"
   or (SyslogMessage has "--percent" and SyslogMessage has "--recursive")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toy Ghouls C2: egress to 89.125.66.101, socks5.exe proxy, reverse SSH tunnel AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts command-and-control activity from the GenieLocker intrusion: outbound connections to the confirmed C2 IP 89.125.66.101, execution of the dropped socks5.exe proxy, and reverse SSH tunnels (ssh -R) used to reach the C2. Anchored on the article's named C2 IP and tooling. Rationale: Uses the article's single named C2 IP (89.125.66.101) plus the named intrusion tooling socks5.exe and the reverse SSH tunnel (ssh -R) described in the Lateral Movement/C2 section. A hardcoded C2 IP match is alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/
ATT&CKT1090 T1572 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned pentest reusing socks5 tooling
  • Legit SSH remote-forward (-R) set up by an admin for a service tunnel
  • Threat-intel/EDR sensor sandbox reaching the IOC IP during analysis
  • Shared-hosting IP reassignment causing benign traffic to 89.125.66.101
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ssh.exe" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-backup","svc-monitor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user for the connection to 89.125.66.101; confirm socks5.exe/ssh -R presence and location. 2) Contain: block the C2 IP at the perimeter, isolate the host, and kill the proxy/tunnel process. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts that resolved or connected to the C2, look for socks5.exe/OpenSSH drops elsewhere, and correlate with GenieLocker execution and PsExec/PAExec deployment.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.125.66.101"
   or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "socks5.exe"
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ssh.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-R")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "89.125.66.101"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, SrcUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toy Ghouls toolset staging: SoftPerfect netscan, socks5.exe proxy, Mimikatz AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the post-access tooling the actor deployed for discovery and credential dumping: SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe), the socks5.exe proxy, and Mimikatz. Anchored on the specific tool names/commands named in the Discovery and Credential Access section. Rationale: Directly uses the named discovery/credential tools from the article: SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe), socks5.exe, and Mimikatz (matched by classic module commands and the gentilkiwi signature to survive renames). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1046 T1003.001 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/network team legitimately running SoftPerfect Network Scanner for inventory
  • Red-team engagement using Mimikatz with authorization
  • Renamed penetration-testing socks proxy used by sanctioned testers
  • EDR/AV quarantine event re-surfacing an old Mimikatz sample name
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "netscan.exe" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-netops","netadmin"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether netscan.exe/socks5.exe/Mimikatz execution was authorized (change ticket / pentest window); capture user, host, and drop path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, reset credentials for any account active on it, and remove the staged binaries. 3) Hunt: pivot to KeePassXC/.kdbx access by the same accounts, RDP/SSH lateral movement, and any subsequent PsExec/PAExec deployment of genie_encrypt.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("netscan.exe","socks5.exe")
   or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "mimikatz.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "gentilkiwi"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","privilege::debug","lsadump::")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("netscan.exe","socks5.exe")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","privilege::debug","lsadump::")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

KeePassXC credential-vault access by non-KeePass process (.kdbx theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts attempts to steal stored credentials from KeePassXC databases, which the actor accessed on multiple compromised hosts. Flags creation/copy/rename of .kdbx vault files by any process other than the KeePass client — the shape of a database being staged for exfil or opened by attacker tooling. Rationale: Anchored on the article's statement that the actor accessed KeePassXC databases on several hosts to extract stored credentials; .kdbx touched by anything other than the KeePass client is a high-fidelity vault-theft signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/
ATT&CKT1555.005 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup software (Veeam, robocopy, OneDrive/Dropbox sync) copying a user's .kdbx
  • User manually copying their vault to a USB/network share
  • IT migrating a profile including the KeePass database
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine engine moving a .kdbx during a scan
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","onedrive.exe","robocopy.exe","dropbox.exe") and ActionType == "FileCreated")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process and account touching the .kdbx and whether it's a known backup/sync tool vs attacker tooling (cmd, powershell, robocopy to a staging dir). 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset every credential known to be stored in that vault. 3) Hunt: correlate with Mimikatz execution on the same host, look for the vault file appearing in temp/staging paths, and check outbound transfer to C2 89.125.66.101.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("keepassxc.exe","keepass.exe","keepassxc-cli.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where ActingProcessName !has "keepass"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("89.125.66.101") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["89.125.66.101"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession

   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] TA488 half-click OWA lure: inbound generic email with no URLs or attachments · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OWAReaper server-side persistence: Owner rights granted to Default user on mailbox folders · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OWAReaper C2 / DNS-tunneled exfil to TA488 actor-controlled domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
OWAReaper server-side persistence: Owner rights granted to Default user on mailbox folders AIInstallation High
Hunts OWAReaper's key persistence act — granting Owner-level permission to the 'Default' (or 'Anonymous') principal on mailbox folders via the OWA web client, so any authenticated org user retains mailbox access after the victim's credential rotation or device re-image. This is the specific server-side backdoor Proofpoint highlights as requiring deliberate Exchange-side removal. Rationale: Directly targets the article's marquee behaviour — OWAReaper 'grants itself Owner-level permissions to the Default user on every mail folder', producing rare UpdateFolderPermissions/AddFolderPermissions events with Default/Anonymous=Owner via the OWA client. Owner-to-Default is almost never legitimate. Cross-checked Proofpoint and BleepingComputer confirming the server-side persistence mechanism. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-exchange-owa-zero-day-for-long-term-mailbox-access/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/30/cve-2026-42897-microsoft-exchange-email-attack/
ATT&CKT1098.002 T1098
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin or migration tooling bulk-resetting folder permissions during mailbox onboarding
  • Legitimate org-wide calendar/free-busy sharing that sets Default to Reviewer (not Owner — refine on Owner)
  • Third-party mailbox delegation/archiving products writing folder ACLs
  • Help-desk troubleshooting of shared-mailbox access
  • Resource-mailbox (room/equipment) auto-accept configuration
Suppression filter
| where ClientInfoString has "OWA" or ClientInfoString has "OutlookWebApp" // scope to the web client OWAReaper runs in
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the OfficeActivity/CloudAppEvents record — confirm grantee is Default/Anonymous with Owner rights and that ClientInfoString/UserAgent indicates OWA. Note MailboxOwnerUPN, ClientIP, and the acting UserId. 2) Contain: Remove the malicious folder permission on every affected folder (Set-MailboxFolderPermission ... -User Default -AccessRights None), then check for and revoke any Add-MailboxPermission/delegate grants; force sign-out and revoke OAuth tokens for the mailbox. Because this persists server-side, credential rotation alone is insufficient. 3) Hunt: Enumerate all mailboxes with Default/Anonymous=Owner org-wide, review the same OWA session for OAuth token theft from add-ins with ReadWriteMailbox, and correlate the acting IP to the exfil-domain UC.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in~ ("UpdateFolderPermissions","AddFolderPermissions","ModifyFolderPermissions","Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has "Owner" and (Raw has "Default" or Raw has "Anonymous")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, IPAddress, UserAgent, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in~ ("UpdateFolderPermissions","AddFolderPermissions","ModifyFolderPermissions","Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| extend Details = strcat(tostring(Parameters), " ", tostring(EventData), " ", ClientInfoString)
| where Details has "Owner" and (Details has "Default" or Details has "Anonymous")
| project TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, UserId, Operation, ClientIP, ClientInfoString, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OWAReaper Mailbox Folder Owner Grant to Default Principal
id: 6b1e2f4a-7c3d-4a8e-9f21-3c9a1d0e77b2
description: Detects granting Owner-level folder permission to the Default or Anonymous principal via OWA, OWAReaper's credential-rotation-surviving persistence.
references:
  - https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-hackers-exploit-microsoft-owa.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1098.002
logsource:
  product: m365
  service: exchange
detection:
  selection:
    Operation:
      - UpdateFolderPermissions
      - AddFolderPermissions
      - ModifyFolderPermissions
  grantee:
    - Default
    - Anonymous
  right:
    - Owner
  condition: selection and grantee and right
level: high
CLOUD
index=o365 sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=Exchange (Operation="UpdateFolderPermissions" OR Operation="AddFolderPermissions" OR Operation="ModifyFolderPermissions" OR Operation="Add-MailboxFolderPermission" OR Operation="Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| eval blob=_raw

OWAReaper C2 / DNS-tunneled exfil to TA488 actor-controlled domains AICommand & Control High
Detects host or browser resolution/connection to the four TA488 exfiltration and C2 domains used by OWAReaper for AES-CTR HTTPS exfil and DNS label tunneling. These infrastructure domains are deliberately named to mimic DNS-resolver services (asecdns, dnsrecursive, tdndns) to blend into normal traffic. Rationale: Uses the four concrete actor-controlled domains (asecdns.com, acocdn.com, dnsrecursive.eu, tdndns.com) named as OWAReaper's HTTPS exfil and DNS-tunnel destinations. Exact-domain IOC match is inherently high-fidelity; the DNS-service-mimicking naming is itself a hunt tell. Campaign infrastructure corroborated via Proofpoint and Help Net Security reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/30/cve-2026-42897-microsoft-exchange-email-attack/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation infrastructure resolving the IOCs during analysis
  • Security scanners or DNS sinkholes proactively querying known-bad domains
  • An internal passive-DNS or blocklist-testing tool enumerating IOC lists
  • Typosquat collision where a benign lookalike shares a base string (verify exact FQDN suffix)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the querying host/user and the initiating process (expect a browser running an OWA tab — msedge.exe/chrome.exe). Confirm the exact FQDN and check query volume/length for DNS-tunnel patterns (long, high-entropy labels). 2) Contain: Block the four domains at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat the associated mailbox as compromised — revoke OAuth tokens and sessions. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the same user to the mailbox-folder-permission persistence UC, review OWA session history for the CVE-2026-42897 exploit email, and sweep the org for any other host resolving these domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("asecdns.com","acocdn.com","dnsrecursive.eu","tdndns.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("asecdns.com","acocdn.com","dnsrecursive.eu","tdndns.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TA488 half-click OWA lure: inbound generic email with no URLs or attachments AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the delivery shape of the CVE-2026-42897 half-click campaign — inbound emails deliberately carrying no URLs and no attachments (payload hidden in social-media-icon HTML), using bland informational lures on supply chain, gas/tourism metrics, nuclear energy and public health, frequently from Proton Mail. Hunting-tier scoping for OWA-exposed recipients. Rationale: Encodes the campaign's distinctive delivery signature confirmed by Proofpoint/multiple outlets: zero-URL, zero-attachment inbound mail (the half-click design that excludes links/attachments) with generic lures (semiconductor supply chain, gas markets, tourism, nuclear, public health) and Proton Mail senders. Deliberately hunting-tier given benign text-only mail is common. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/ta488-outlook-half-click-owareaper/
ATT&CKT1566 T1203
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate industry newsletters/analyst briefs on gas, tourism or semiconductor markets with no links
  • Internal or partner informational notices sent as plain text
  • Automated report digests whose subjects contain 'metrics' or 'research update'
  • Proton Mail users legitimately corresponding with the org
  • Marketing preview/plain-text A-B test messages
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("mailchimp.com","sendgrid.net","amazonses.com","mailgun.org")) // strip known bulk-mail ESPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: For hits, prioritise recipients whose mailboxes are OWA/on-prem-Exchange accessible (CVE-2026-42897 targets on-prem OWA). Inspect raw message HTML for onload= handlers and Base64 fragments after '#' inside <img> social-icon elements. 2) Contain: Quarantine/soft-delete matching messages tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, and confirm Exchange is patched for CVE-2026-42897. 3) Hunt: For any recipient who opened the mail in OWA, pivot to the mailbox-folder-permission persistence UC and the actor-domain exfil UC to determine whether OWAReaper executed.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where UrlCount == 0 and AttachmentCount == 0
| where Subject has_any ("supply chain","semiconductor","gas market","gas markets","tourism","nuclear","public health","research update","metrics")
| extend ProtonSender = (SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("proton.me","protonmail.com","pm.me") or SenderFromDomain in~ ("proton.me","protonmail.com","pm.me"))
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, ProtonSender, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where UrlCount == 0 and AttachmentCount == 0
| where Subject has_any ("supply chain","semiconductor","gas market","gas markets","tourism","nuclear","public health","research update","metrics")
| extend ProtonSender = (SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("proton.me","protonmail.com","pm.me") or SenderFromDomain in~ ("proton.me","protonmail.com","pm.me"))
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, ProtonSender, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryLocation
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or SHA1 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or MD5 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or SHA1 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or MD5 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm registry look-alike phishing domains (npmjs.help / npmjs.store) in mail & web · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Amazon Links Debug and Chalk npm Hijack to North Korea’s Sapphire Sleet
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Known Sapphire Sleet npm payload hashes written or executed · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Sapphire Sleet npm supply-chain C2 egress to npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Sapphire Sleet npm supply-chain C2 egress to npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the DPRK-attributed npm supply-chain C2 (domain npmjs.store, IP 216.74.123.126) tied to the trojanized debug/chalk/axios/typo-crypto packages. npmjs.store is a registry look-alike that is never a legitimate npm endpoint (real registry is registry.npmjs.org / npmjs.com), so a hit is a high-fidelity compromise signal on a developer or CI/CD host. Rationale: Uses the two network IOCs Amazon published (domain npmjs.store, IP 216.74.123.126). npmjs.store is a registry look-alike with no legitimate use, giving near-zero baseline noise. Cross-checked BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and the AWS Security blog which all list the same infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-identifies-north-korean-hacker-group-behind-open-source-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/amazon-links-debug-chalk-npm-supply-chain-attacks-to-north-korean-hackers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/amazon-links-debug-and-chalk-npm-hijack.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or CI sandbox detonating a compromised package sample and resolving the C2 on purpose
  • Threat-intel enrichment/crawler tooling (e.g. urlscan agents) resolving npmjs.store from a SOC egress host
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS appliance logging the query as it blackholes it
  • IP 216.74.123.126 later reassigned by its shared-hosting provider to a benign tenant, generating stale-IOC hits
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 Triage: identify the process that made the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine) — expect node.exe, npm, a build agent, or a browser; confirm whether the host recently ran `npm install` / has debug/chalk/axios in a lockfile. Step 2 Contain: isolate the host, block npmjs.store + 216.74.123.126 at proxy/firewall/protective-DNS, and rotate any crypto-wallet keys, npm tokens and cloud credentials that touched the machine. Step 3 Hunt: pull package-lock.json/yarn.lock across the fleet for compromised versions, sweep all endpoints for the two known SHA256 payloads, and review CI/CD build logs for the C2 during the Sep-2025 / Mar-2026 windows.
let c2domain = "npmjs.store";
let c2ip = "216.74.123.126";
union
 (DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has c2domain or RemoteIP == c2ip
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Src="NetworkConnect"),
 (DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where RemoteUrl has c2domain or AdditionalFields has c2ip
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, Src="DnsQuery")
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2domain = "npmjs.store";
let c2ip = "216.74.123.126";
union isfuzzy=true
 (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has c2domain | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, Indicator=c2domain, Src="DNS"),
 (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == c2ip or DstHostname has c2domain | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Indicator=iff(DstIpAddr==c2ip, c2ip, c2domain), Src="Network"),
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationHostName has c2domain or DestinationIP == c2ip or RequestURL has c2domain | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL, Indicator=c2domain, Src="Proxy")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Sapphire Sleet npm payload hashes written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the two malicious SHA256 payloads Amazon tied to the trojanized npm packages, on either file-write or process-execution. A match means the second-stage payload from the debug/chalk/axios/typo-crypto compromise landed on an endpoint or build agent. Rationale: Uses the two exact SHA256 IOCs from Amazon's report (typo-crypto package hash + trojanized core.js hash) as file-write and execution pivots — hash matches are deterministic and effectively FP-free. Distinct log-source pivot (file/hash) from the network UC. Verified against the AWS Security blog IOC list. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-identifies-north-korean-hacker-group-behind-open-source-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/amazon-links-debug-chalk-npm-supply-chain-attacks-to-north-korean-hackers/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR quarantine or sample-submission tooling copying the payload into a vault path (still worth reviewing)
  • A malware-analysis or reverse-engineering VM where an analyst intentionally staged the sample
  • Backup/DLP indexer re-hashing a previously quarantined artifact
Response runbook
Step 1 Triage: confirm the hash hit is a live artifact vs. an EDR quarantine copy; capture the FolderPath and the writing/executing process. Step 2 Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the file, and revoke npm tokens, SSH keys and crypto-wallet material accessible from it. Step 3 Hunt: enumerate every host that installed debug/chalk/axios/typo-crypto in the affected version windows, and pivot on the same devices for outbound npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126 traffic to scope C2 reach.

npm registry look-alike phishing domains (npmjs.help / npmjs.store) in mail & web AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the maintainer-phishing look-alike domains used to hijack npm maintainer accounts (npmjs.help credential-harvest page, npmjs.store) arriving via email links or being browsed. Targets the initial-access step Amazon described as 'socially engineering package maintainers' — catching your own developers being lured with the same kit. Rationale: Combines the C2/registry look-alike npmjs.store (Amazon) with the corroborated maintainer-phishing domain npmjs.help documented by Aikido and Semgrep for the Sep-2025 debug/chalk hijack. Different pivot (email/URL-click/web, initial access) from the network and hash UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-debug-and-chalk-packages-compromised • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2025/chalk-debug-and-color-on-npm-compromised-in-new-supply-chain-attack/ • https://cycode.com/blog/npm-debug-chalk-supply-chain-attack-the-complete-guide/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness or phishing-simulation platform seeding these domains in a test campaign
  • SOC analyst manually browsing the domain during threat research from a corporate egress
  • Brand-protection / takedown vendor probing the look-alike domain
  • Threat-intel feed pre-fetching the URL for enrichment
Response runbook
Step 1 Triage: identify the recipient/user and whether a click occurred (IsClickedThrough) and whether credentials were submitted; check if the user is a package maintainer or holds npm publish rights. Step 2 Contain: block npmjs.help + npmjs.store at mail gateway and proxy, force-reset the user's npm and SSO credentials, and revoke active npm publish tokens. Step 3 Hunt: search mail flow for the same sender/URL across the org, review recent npm publish events for maintainer accounts, and pivot any clicking host to the C2/hash UCs to confirm downstream compromise.

 (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d) | where DnsQuery has_any ("npmjs.help", "npmjs.store") | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, Src="DNS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or SHA1 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or MD5 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or SHA1 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or MD5 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added a newly disclosed security flaw impacting Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) Software to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of zero-day exploitation. The vulnerability, assigned CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS score: 5.3), could permit an unauthenticated, remote attacker to log
